origin: The Collective Service is a global partnership for risk communication and community engagement in health emergencies. Its website was set up in 2020 as a central library of guidance, and it is still the partnership’s front door: the place coordinators and responders go for tools, training and data when they have to reach communities during an outbreak.

Six years on, the site was still shaped by the pandemic it was built for. Most of its library dated from 2020 to 2022, while the emergencies people were working on had moved on. The people who most needed it were also the hardest to reach, often on a phone and a slow connection.

I did not start with a design. I started by reading: the site’s own database, an independent evaluation of the partnership, and the published research on how people in crises find and use guidance. Every rule on the new site goes back to that reading, and each one is labelled with the kind of support it has, so anyone can challenge it.

intro: A review of comparable platforms and published studies produced thirteen findings that survived a three-way check of each claim. It also stated its limits: no study looked at these coordinators directly, and nothing verified covered look and feel. So the design says where it rests on evidence and where it is my judgement, open to challenge and to testing with responders.

items.title: What already worked
items.text: A 2023 independent evaluation, built on 88 interviews and 98 survey responses, found the site’s online resources were the partnership’s best-rated product, at about 80 out of 100. So the library, the kits and the dashboards stayed at the centre. I changed how things are found, dated and labelled, not what the site is.

items.title: Slow connections are real, but not universal
items.text: In a 2022 survey of people sharing emergency-health course content, poor connectivity was the most-cited difficulty in low-income countries, at 29%, against 8% in high-income countries, while 47% reported no difficulty at all. The median home page on a phone was 2.56 MB in 2025, about 51 seconds at 400 kilobits per second. So the site is built for the slow connection first: pages are light, and a document can be read in the browser before anyone has to download it.

items.title: People say finding things is easy, then complain about search
items.text: One comparable hub reports that 92% of people found resources easily, yet 18% of its open comments are about usability, mainly search, navigation and downloads. A user test of another found the lack of a search box on the home page to be one of its two big problems. So search sits in the header of every page, and a satisfaction score is not accepted as proof.

items.title: Field teams want less, not more
items.text: The evaluation found more guidance being produced than country teams could absorb, and suggested fewer, shorter documents. A study of staff in three crisis-affected countries found short documents preferred, and a 140-page handbook judged too long to navigate. So each kit opens with a “Start here” selection of up to four documents.

items.title: Guidance goes stale, and trust depends on showing your working
items.text: In a 2020 review of 131 humanitarian guidance documents, only 18% had been updated since they were published. Trust is among the benefits users of comparable hubs cite most. So every document shows who published it and when, and every link is checked automatically. Research does not yet show which signals create trust, so this is my best reading of it, and it stays open to testing.

items.title: People pass things on
items.text: Among 819 people who shared course content, 60% shared a link, 36% used WhatsApp and 26% reformatted it for SMS or WhatsApp. So the website cannot be the only channel. Every document and kit has a short, stable address and a preview that explains itself when pasted into a chat.

items.title: Language is a recurring gap
items.text: All 131 of those guidance documents were in English, and only 28% were also in French. So each document appears once, with its other languages together on the same page.

intro: One rule sat behind the design: when audiences conflict, responders win. Most of what follows comes from that sentence. The colours were worked out with a perceptual colour model and the WCAG contrast formula, and the type, spacing and tap targets were set against published research, so each choice below has a reason that can be checked.

items.title: Why the weight limit came first
items.text: Every page had to stay under 500 KB, about 10 seconds at 400 kilobits per second. That limit was set before any design, so every template was built to it. Each download states its format and size before it is pressed, because a responder on a metered connection decides whether to spend the data before pressing, not after.

items.title: Why the palette is built on lightness
items.text: About 8% of men have red-green colour blindness, and a photocopier cannot see colour at all. Lightness survives both. So the palette sits in three separate bands on the OKLCH lightness scale of 0 to 100: dark inks at 20 to 46, corals at 49 to 76 and page colours at 90 to 100. In a colour-blindness simulation coral turns olive, but a coral button on sand stays readable, because the difference in lightness remains.

items.title: Why coral means only one thing
items.text: Ink and sand have almost no colour in them. Coral has about five times as much, so wherever it appears the eye finds it first. That lets coral carry a meaning: what is live now, or the one action that matters on a page. Decision time grows with the number of equally weighted choices, an effect known as Hick’s law, so each view spends coral on one action only.

items.title: Why the page is sand and the text is ink
items.text: A sand page sends about 7% less light to the eye than white, which eases glare in long reading, and text on it still reaches a contrast of 15 to 1. White is kept for cards and fields, so a white box reads as the place to type. Text is a blue-black ink, not pure black, so text, dark bands and photo overlays are one colour at different strengths, cool against a warm ground.

items.title: Why every colour pair was computed
items.text: White text on one coral measures 3.63 to 1, which fails the 4.5 to 1 that body text needs. On a slightly darker coral it reaches 4.89, so that is the coral the buttons use. Every text and background pair was worked out the same way. The same care keeps the identity clear of the partners’ own colours: ink has so little colour that it reads as a neutral, and coral is neither the red nor the orange they use.

items.title: Why text is 17 pixels and lines stop at about 70 characters
items.text: Reviews of reading research put the lower edge of fluent reading at around 16 pixels at normal screen distance, and a 104-person eye-tracking study found comprehension improved as type grew. So body text is 17 pixels and never below 16 on a phone. Reading on screen is most comfortable at about 45 to 75 characters a line, so the column holds about 66 to 70. Line spacing is 1.55, just above the 1.5 recommended by the British Dyslexia Association and used as the test in WCAG.

items.title: Why headings are sentences, set in a serif
items.text: Text set entirely in capitals is read 10 to 20% more slowly, because word shapes flatten into rectangles, so capitals are kept for short labels and badges. Headings are written as sentences because a scanning reader then gets the point from the heading alone. A serif for headings and a sans for everything else gives two clear voices from only two font families, which matters because fonts are the one asset that can hold back text.

items.title: Why everything is at least 44 pixels to tap
items.text: The accessibility standard’s minimum is 24 pixels. I took 44 as the floor, because the main audience uses the site one-handed on a phone, often walking or in a vehicle. A study of thumb use on small touchscreens found errors fell sharply up to about 9.2 millimetres, roughly 44 pixels.

items.title: Why the shapes are rounded
items.text: People judge curved shapes as more pleasant and less threatening than sharp ones. The effect is small but consistent, and a site built for people under stress should use it. Shape also does a job: pills are only for things that can be pressed, cards hold things to read, and fields are squarer, so a field never looks like a button.

items.title: Why the motion is quiet
items.text: Motion has three jobs: to show where something came from, to confirm that a control responded and to signal that a response is live. A response feels instant at about a tenth of a second, and thought flows unbroken up to about one second, so movement stays close to that range. Anyone who asks their device for less motion gets none.

items.title: Why the photographs are documentary
items.text: Photography is evidence here, not decoration. The brand asks for real people doing the work, such as a conversation, a radio spot or a training room, in daylight and at eye level, credited as carefully as a cited document. There are no staged metaphors such as handshakes or globes, and no close-ups of distress.

intro: Everything the Service publishes speaks in one voice, with four rules: plain, concrete, calm and honest. They exist for one reader: someone in the middle of an emergency who has no time to decode a sentence.

items.title: Why the language is plain
items.text: Short sentences, everyday words and active verbs, because jargon is a barrier to someone in the middle of a crisis. The site says what is happening and what to do next.

items.title: Why there are numbers instead of adjectives
items.text: Claims are counts. “39 documents are ready for this response” persuades; “a wealth of resources” does not. Headings carry a fact, never a label such as “Our resources”.

items.title: Why it stays calm
items.text: Urgency comes from clarity, never from volume. There are no exclamation marks, no capitals for emphasis and no alarm language outside the alert itself. In an active emergency the words get shorter, not louder: instructions and counts first, with no adjectives.

items.title: Why some words are not used
items.text: Beneficiaries, target audience, leverage, solutions, empower, comprehensive, world-class and innovative are all left out. People are communities with agency, not recipients, and if a word could open a pitch deck it does not belong here.

items.title: Why the tone changes from page to page
items.text: There is one voice and four registers. An active emergency gets the shortest sentences. The library is factual. About is the one place for history. The Helpdesk speaks directly to “you”, because that is where the reader acts.

items.title: Why buttons say what will happen
items.text: “Open the kit” and “Send the request” tell a reader what comes next; “Submit” and “Go” do not. Error messages work the same way: they say what is wrong and what to do, such as “The deadline is before today. Choose a later date.”

items.title: Why it admits what is missing
items.text: The voice labels what is draft or missing and invites correction: “Ask for something we are missing” is part of the brand, not an apology. Dates are written out, as in 4 Sep 2025, because 04/09 means two different days on two continents.

decisions.title: Rebuild from the ground up
decisions.text: Updating the old site page by page would have kept the structure and weight it needed to lose. So every page was rebuilt: a custom WordPress theme of 30 page templates, a new editing side, and content brought across through a repeatable importer that can be rerun and checked.

decisions.title: Hold every document on the site
decisions.text: Many documents were only linked to, so they would stop working if a publisher moved a page. I fetched 155 of them, so the site now holds its own copies, with French, Portuguese, Spanish and Swahili versions where publishers offer them. Documents listed two, three or four times now appear once, with their other languages on the same page.

decisions.title: Build for the people who will run it
decisions.text: A library only stays current if its own team can keep it current. The editing side has one form for each kind of content, and each form lists what is still missing before it can be published. Adding a document means pasting its address: its format, size and page count fill in by themselves. A built-in guide shows editors each job, screen by screen.

decisions.title: Try a new way into the library
decisions.text: Search only helps people who know the right words. The Knowledge bank lets a reader describe a situation in their own words and get advice drawn only from the library’s documents, with every point cited. When the library has no answer, it says so.

intro: The new identity began with the partnership’s own evidence, not with the logo. A 2023 independent evaluation, built on 88 interviews, 98 survey responses and four country case studies, found the name “confusing for some” and listed “limited communication about its purpose” as a weakness. It also found that 87% of respondents thought they were likely to need the Service in a future health emergency. So this had to be an identity built to last, and one that helps explain what the Service is.

The existing logo was made to put a name on a pandemic response, and it did that job. It had not been asked to do more. A logo that is only the name cannot explain a name people find confusing, so the identity needed a form that carries the idea: organisations acting as one, so that communities are listened to in an emergency.

reasons.title: It says what the Service is
reasons.text: Three separate parts join one body: distinct organisations, drawn as equals, becoming one service. A reader sees “together” before reading a word, so the mark works on the confusion the evaluation found every time it appears.

reasons.title: It is a shape the sector has not used
reasons.text: Three bars and a block is specific and ownable. It is not a globe, a hand, a heart or a cross, the shapes the humanitarian sector has already used up. The joined body is drawn to the width of the parts that form it, because nothing is added when organisations combine: the whole is the parts, joined.

reasons.title: It keeps the partners equal
reasons.text: The Service is a partnership of equals. No part of the mark takes precedence, and a single quiet colour lets it sit beside four established logos without crowding them.

reasons.title: It matches how the partners work
reasons.text: Each partner pairs a symbol with its name. The Service was the only member of its own partnership without one.

reasons.title: It works in every language
reasons.text: The Service publishes in English, French, Portuguese and Spanish, and much of its work is in francophone and lusophone Africa. A symbol works in all of them. The name stays in English and the line beneath it is translated.

reasons.title: It works wherever the Service appears
reasons.text: The Service is increasingly found in feeds, browser tabs, group chats and on phones, where a wordmark cannot be read. Solid shapes also survive the stamps, badges and photocopies of field materials. Size was only one test of eight. Both logos were tested on meaning, small sizes, reusable parts, sitting with the partners, matching the voice, reliable reproduction, distinctiveness and whether rules can govern them.

reasons.title: It survives a change of name
reasons.text: The evaluation recommended that the partners consider changing the name. If they do, the mark stays and only the words beside it change.

reasons.title: It rests on evidence, at low risk
reasons.text: A 2019 study in the Journal of Marketing Research, across six experiments and 597 logos, found that more descriptive logos are easier to take in and are judged more authentic, most of all for brands people do not yet know well. The cost of changing is low: the name, where the recognition lives, stays, and the mark is one small file using fonts the site already loads. The risk of not changing is that the evaluation’s findings stay unaddressed at the most visible layer.

guidelines: The identity goes further than the mark. The voice, the colours and the photography described above all belong to it.

All of this is set out in a 57-page design and brand document, shared with the partnership in October 2026. Part A makes the case and sets the guidelines: the evidence, the side-by-side tests, the cost and risk of changing, voice and tone, construction, clear space and minimum sizes, colour, type, photography, four language versions, use beside the partners and the rules. Part B is the design standard for the website, and every rule in it carries its reason and the kind of support behind it: the terms of reference, published evidence, a computed value, a standard or my own judgement.
The identity is proposed and is shared here with the partnership’s permission; adopting it is the partnership’s decision.

results: The site has not launched, so there are no visitor results to report yet. Until the relaunch, the partnership’s public address still shows the old site.

What can be reported is what was tested. On 23 October 2026 a crawl of 332 pages and 634 links to other sites found none broken. Every page is checked from 320 to 1,920 pixels wide. Visitor measurement is built in and loads only after a visitor consents, so the relaunch can be judged on real use.
lessons: Count before you design. Reading the site’s own database, rather than estimating from a crawl, showed how much of the library belonged to another time, and that changed the plan.
Weight is a design decision. Set the limit first and every template is built to it.
Make the case for a brand with evidence. Setting out the findings, the tests and the cost of change lets partners decide on the argument, not on taste.
Show people real pages. Reviewers pinned comments to the working site, so each point was about something they could see and could be tracked to a fix or a decision.

origin: The Global Girls Foundation is a Swiss foundation, established in 2022, created by Plan International to fund its programmes for girls. It describes itself as the platform for global philanthropists, and it wants them to feel part of a mission, not simply donors to a charity.

Its website did not say that. It was 11 pages on Plan International’s shared WordPress platform, hard to manage and to find things on. It told strong stories but gave no clear next step, and it had no integrated way to give.

The new site had two jobs that pull in different directions. It had to read as a serious institution to someone thinking about a legacy or an endowment, and it still had to take a gift by card from anyone who wanted to give today.

intro: I started by asking. Three questionnaires went out in June 2026, one each for donors, stakeholders and the Foundation’s team. The answers were consistent enough to design from, so the interviews I had planned were not needed.

items.title: Who the site is really for
items.text: Six donor audiences were named at the start, and one came first: a philanthropist and the people around them, such as a family office, an adviser or a lawyer. I wrote that down and judged every decision against it. For this reader, proof means governance, audited accounts and what a gift achieves at scale. Small-gift habits such as urgency banners would cheapen that, so they were left out.

items.title: What the first seconds have to do
items.text: One answer set the bar for the home page: within seconds, a visitor should realise how much investing in girls can achieve. Another pointed to the gap in the old site: strong storytelling, but no clear next step. So the page had to make the case fast and then offer somewhere to go.

items.title: Three ways to open the home page
items.text: I built three working home pages, led by impact, by a girl’s story and by a flagship programme, and the Foundation’s team and a youth delegate compared them. The impact opening built credibility at once. The story drew people in, but worked best in support. Opening on one programme risked making the Foundation look like a single initiative. So the final page opens on a bold statement, brings in the figures straight after, and uses stories in support.

items.title: The question every first-time visitor asks
items.text: The team pointed out that a new visitor would ask: why this Foundation, and how is it different from Plan International? So the line “The philanthropic arm of Plan International” sits in the opening screen, because the connection builds credibility, and the Why girls page asks the question outright: why this, and not a general gift?

items.title: Plan International’s brand rules
items.text: I read Plan’s 104-page Global Brand Manual and checked the design against it. The manual names the Foundation as an example of an external campaign that may carry an aligned identity, with Plan’s logo leading. Every point where the design departs from the manual is written down in a register, with the reason and its status, ready to hand to Plan’s brand team.

items.title: How Plan’s own national sites work
items.text: I also looked at what Plan’s strongest fundraising sites actually do. Some use rounded buttons and cards, and one puts a giving control in the header. That showed what could work for a donor while still belonging to the brand.

intro: The design had to feel like a serious institution and still belong to Plan International. Each choice below comes from the reader, from Plan’s brand rules or from a measured value, and all of it is set out in a design standard of 19 parts.

items.title: Why the first screen offers two routes
items.text: A major gift usually starts with a conversation. So the first screen offers two routes side by side: give now, or start a conversation. The Annual Giving Fund and the endowment are reached only through a conversation, and the giving panel names who to talk to, because this reader expects a person, not a form.

items.title: Why giving opens over the page
items.text: The giving panel opens from the header on every page instead of sending people somewhere else. It is always within reach, and the page the donor was reading stays behind it, so they never lose their place.

items.title: Why Plan Blue leads and yellow means give
items.text: Plan’s manual says its blue takes precedence and that no more than three colours should appear at once. Yellow cannot carry text: on white it measures 1.42 to 1, far below the 4.5 to 1 that body text needs. So yellow is only ever a fill or a mark, and the giving button is the button that wears it.

items.title: Why white text is always pure white
items.text: On Plan Blue, pure white measures 4.89 to 1, which passes. Fade it to 74% and it falls to about 3.4 to 1, which fails. So hierarchy on blue comes from size and weight, never from fading the text.

items.title: Why each typeface has one job
items.text: Poppins Bold carries structure and Arial carries reading, as Plan’s manual asks. Georgia italic is kept for captions and sources, and it never runs at heading size, because on this site it is the voice of a caveat and a title in it would read as provisional. Running text stops at 68 characters a line, inside the readable band of 45 to 75.

items.title: Why the corners are rounded, against the manual
items.text: Plan’s manual recommends square corners, but its strongest fundraising sites use rounded ones, and the manual’s word is “recommend”, not “must”. So the site follows that live practice, records the departure and gives corners a rule: pills for controls, soft corners for cards, and square for photographs that meet the page edge and for supplied logos.

items.title: Why the photographs show girls doing things
items.text: Plan’s manual asks images to show agency, knowledge and resilience, not to portray people as victims. So the rule is girls doing something, not being helped, with faces fully in frame. Visible distress and rescue framing are left out. Portraits are square, not circular, because a circle crops the jaw, and the opening photograph has its own crop for each screen shape so a face is never cut.

items.title: Why the detail sits in the footer
items.text: An adviser looks for the facts: registration, audit, bank details. They sit in the footer of every page, so the top of each page stays clear and the facts are always one scroll away. Detail lives at the bottom, where it helps the person looking for it and does not overwhelm the person who is not.

items.title: Why there are only ten text styles
items.text: The first concept had grown to 56 font sizes. Each began as a reasonable local decision, and the count is what happens when local decisions are allowed. The standard cut that to ten text styles, six text colours and four corner radii, and custom sizes, colours and spacing are switched off in WordPress, so an editor cannot bring the drift back.

items.title: Why everything moves slowly
items.text: Every element moves in one consistent way, slowly enough to be seen, so the site feels considered, not static. It has limits: no face moves, nothing follows the cursor, and anyone who asks their device for less motion gets none.

intro: The Foundation has the final say on its own words. My part was to give those words a clear logic and to make sure every sentence stayed true.

items.title: Why the site talks about investing
items.text: The opening line is “Investing in girls is the smartest thing the world can do.” This reader, and the adviser beside them, weigh a gift as a use of capital, so the site uses that language: capital, returns, compounding. The case for giving is headed “Be right, not just generous.” It separates the Foundation from a traditional charity model, as its team asked.

items.title: Why “platform”, not “community”
items.text: In an early review I suggested describing the Foundation as a community. The Foundation pointed out that in German the word can sound basic, and the site would one day be in German. So the opening line calls it “the platform for global philanthropists”, which leaves no room for misreading and suits this audience better.

items.title: Why every figure names its source
items.text: “133M girls are out of school worldwide” is followed by the report and page it came from. An adviser will check. The Foundation is also young, so most figures are Plan International’s or come from published research, and the site says so.

items.title: Why the numbers are not the last word
items.text: “The numbers make the case. She is the point.” The team wanted girls at the heart of the site, and Plan’s manual asks for the same. So the evidence leads, and the writing keeps returning to one girl and one decision: whether she goes back to school after the water recedes.

items.title: Why the name is spelled out
items.text: The site says Global Girls Foundation in full, never the initials, because first-time visitors do not know them.

items.title: Why the button says “Give now”
items.text: The buttons first read “Start investing”. The Foundation asked for “Give now”, and that is what every button opening the giving panel now says. The endowment page kept its own wording, because that panel takes no payment and “Give now” would have been untrue.

items.title: Why nothing untrue goes in
items.text: The Foundation decides what it says, with one limit: a sentence that would be false is not published. When the card limit was removed, every sentence that mentioned it was rewritten in the same piece of work. The site still does not say there is no limit, because Stripe and a donor’s own bank have limits of their own.

items.title: Why bank transfer is a quiet line
items.text: Card fees on a very large gift are real money. So a line sits under the amount box at every size: “Prefer to give by bank transfer?” It is a choice for the donor, never a push.

decisions.title: Give the Foundation its own site
decisions.text: Plan International’s platform serves a whole network of sites, so a structural change or a new integration has to suit all of them. The Foundation needed its own giving panel and payment provider, so it moved to its own WordPress site. The brand, safeguarding, accessibility and data protection stayed the same.

decisions.title: Let the donor name the amount
decisions.text: Earlier versions offered preset gift levels. After seeing them, the Foundation asked for them to go, so the giving panel opens with one empty box and sets no upper limit of its own. A gift above what a card can carry shows the bank details instead, and any donor can ask for those at any size.

decisions.title: Keep card details off the site
decisions.text: One-time gifts are taken on the page itself and monthly gifts on Stripe’s hosted page, so card details are handled by Stripe and never by the site. The panel still works as a plain form if scripts are turned off.

decisions.title: Build the editor around the page
decisions.text: The Foundation’s staff needed to run the site themselves. Editors work on the page as it will appear: they change text in place, add sections from a picture menu, and the site checks each page against its rules before it publishes. The WordPress admin was restyled in the Foundation’s own look, with a 31-step guide kept inside it.

decisions.title: Review real pages, not pictures
decisions.text: The design was built as a working review site with comments on the page. The Foundation’s team reviewed real pages on real screens, and only approved pages moved to WordPress.

decisions.title: Move without losing the old addresses
decisions.text: The Foundation’s domain sat with Plan International, so the move depended on its IT team. I sent the exact changes needed, and every old address was set to redirect to its new home. On launch day all 21 pages and 23 redirects answered correctly.

results: The site went live on 9 October 2026, with all 21 pages and 23 redirects answering correctly on the day. One-time and monthly gifts were both confirmed with real payments by 12 October.
For the first time the Foundation can take a gift on its own site, and its staff have been trained to run the pages themselves. Giving totals belong to the Foundation and are not published here.
lessons: Decide who the site is for, then let that settle the arguments. Knowing the reader was a philanthropist made most questions about wording and giving easier to answer.
Expect the giving rules to change. Gift levels, limits and currencies all changed close to launch, so the giving panel had to be easy to change.
When a launch depends on another organisation’s team, send the exact change, not a general request.

standards.label: Accessibility
standards.value: Lighthouse accessibility 100 on the live home and giving pages, 4 November 2026. An axe-core run across 16 pages before launch found no confirmed violations. No screen-reader test by a person is on record yet.

standards.label: Performance
standards.value: Home page 546 KB, giving page 395 KB, measured 4 November 2026. On a 3G profile of 400 kbit/s and 2 s latency the home page shows first content at 6.8 s and its main content at 12.5 s, and is fully loaded at 14.0 s.

standards.label: Security
standards.value: Hosted in Belgium on WP Engine · HTTPS with HSTS · daily backup points · card details held by Stripe

projects.next: Pages in German and French, translated by machine and checked by the Foundation’s team before anything is published.

proves.title: I launch on the day I say.
proves.text: All 21 pages and 23 redirects answered correctly on 9 October 2026, and real one-time and monthly gifts were confirmed by 12 October.

proves.title: Accessibility is measured, not promised.
proves.text: Lighthouse accessibility 100 on the live home and giving pages; an axe-core run across 16 pages found no confirmed violations.

proves.title: Card details never touch the site.
proves.text: One-time gifts on the page and monthly gifts on Stripe’s hosted page, so the site holds no card data to protect.

proves.title: I work with the other organisation’s IT team.
proves.text: The domain sat with Plan International. I sent the exact changes needed, and every old address reached its new home.

proves.title: Your team runs it afterwards.
proves.text: Editors change text on the page itself, with a 31-step guide inside the admin. What is not done is written down too: no screen-reader test by a person is on record yet.

projects.name: Community Trust Index
projects.scope: Website design, WordPress build, interactive map and country data pages
projects.line: Research platform · 2024 · Built from scratch, with a world map, one page design for every country and four languages.
projects.summary: A measure of community trust lived in a spreadsheet that only researchers could read. I designed and built its home from scratch, with a world map, one page design for every country and four languages.

detailImage.alt: The Countries page of the Community Trust Index: a grey world map with red markers, and a count of 17 countries at the top right.
detailImage.caption: The Countries page opens on the map, so a reader sees the reach of the work first.

figures.label: Country reports on the site, up from at least five pages in August 2024, all on the same page design
Study types, Institutional and Early Warning, sharing one page so a country stays in one place
Languages, so results can reach teams who don’t work in English

origin: Trust decides whether people act on what humanitarian organisations tell them. The Community Trust Index measures that trust. It was developed by the IFRC’s Community Engagement and Accountability unit as an evidence-based tool for organisations and the communities they serve.

By early 2024 the results were tracked in a spreadsheet. That worked for the research team and for nobody else. National Societies run the survey, but programme teams and leaders need to read the results and act on them, and a spreadsheet can’t do that.
The Index needed a home of its own, so I designed and built one from scratch.

intro: The site’s structure comes from the method it has to explain. Before drawing a page, I had to understand how a trust score is made and who reads it.

items.title: How the score works
items.text: Answers from several survey questions convert to a common scale of 1 to 10, where 10 is the highest trust. “Don’t know” answers are left out so they don’t affect the result. Question areas then combine into one figure, with the more central aspects of trust given more weight. So the site has to show that single figure and also what sits behind it.

items.title: Why one number is not enough
items.text: Trust is measured through competencies and values, so a page can’t stop at a score. A reader has to see which part of trust is strong and which is weak.

items.title: Why countries need more than one study
items.text: Some countries measure trust in the institution. Others measure trust in early warning systems, across four pillars from risk knowledge to response. A country can have both, so the page had to hold more than one study.

items.title: Why time matters
items.text: Surveys repeat, so a country needs more than one year on a page, and a way to see the change between them.

intro: The design had to do two things: make a research method readable, and make it clear that this tool belongs to the movement that uses it.

items.title: Why the map comes first
items.text: The first question a reader has is whether their country is there, and the first thing a global index has to prove is its reach. The Countries page follows the order the computer scientist Ben Shneiderman set out in 1996 for reading large sets of information: overview first, then zoom and filter, then details on demand. The map gives the overview, the filter narrows it to one study type, and each country page holds the detail. On a phone a world map shrinks past the point of use, so the page leads with the list of reports instead.

items.title: Why every country uses the same page
items.text: Overview, key insights, overall score, then the detail, in that order every time. Edward Tufte’s work on repeated designs explains why: when the layout stays constant, readers stop learning the page and start noticing the data. Someone who has read Zambia can read Nepal, and the differences they see are differences in trust, not in design.

items.title: Why a switch and not a second page
items.text: Nepal has both an Institutional and an Early Warning study. A simple switch moves between them, with tabs for each year and for trends, so a country stays in one place as its evidence grows.

items.title: Why navy and red
items.text: The colours align the Index with the Red Cross and the IFRC, so readers inside the movement recognise it as theirs. Red is kept for emphasis: the key words in a headline and the markers on the map. Navy on white reaches a contrast of 14.6 to 1 and body text 5.6 to 1, both well past the 4.5 to 1 that WCAG AA asks for. The red reaches 4.1 to 1, which meets the 3 to 1 for large text, so it stays on large headings and never carries body text.

items.title: Why people come first, in a soft shape
items.text: The home page opens on a person, not a chart, because trust is about people. The photograph sits in an arch rather than a hard box. In a 2006 study, Moshe Bar and Maital Neta found that people prefer curved objects to sharp-angled ones, which suits a page about trust.

intro: The findings were written with the research team, partly from the data in the sheets.

items.title: Why findings are sentences
items.text: They are statements, not chart labels: “Transparency is the clear trust gap” and “Receiving support does not automatically translate into high trust”. A leader can repeat a sentence like that in a meeting, and a reader who only skims the page still leaves with the finding.

items.title: Why the site names its readers
items.text: The home page speaks to two groups directly: “For programs & operations” and “For leadership”. Each can find what is meant for them without reading the method first.

decisions.title: Build a custom theme
decisions.text: The site runs on a custom WordPress theme, not a template. A map, country data and modules are too specific for a theme bought off the shelf.

decisions.title: Keep content in structured forms
decisions.text: Countries, modules and findings go into fields, not page designs, so every new report takes the same shape without design work.

decisions.title: Read the spreadsheet that already exists
decisions.text: The research team’s Google Sheet already held all the data, so the charts read from it directly. Nothing had to be rebuilt or entered twice, which kept the cost down.

decisions.title: Draw the map from geographic data
decisions.text: Each country on the map has a marker and a link to its page, so the map works as the site’s main way in.

results: The site grew without a redesign. A public archive copy shows at least five country pages in August 2024. There are 14 country reports today, and 17 countries on the counter.

It is in active use: seven of the 14 reports are dated between November 2025 and June 2026, from Slovakia to Madagascar. Early Warning joined Institutional with the same page structure, and Nepal now carries both.
The evidence behind it is large and specific. In Nepal, 5,309 people took part in the Early Warning survey, and 4,958 were included in the analysis.
lessons: Use what already exists. Reading the team’s own spreadsheet saved money and kept the researchers working in a tool they knew.
Keep a copy of anything you depend on. A site that reads an outside file inherits that file’s risks. On the next build, the site would keep its own regular copy of the data.
Design for the next study, not this one. A page built around one study would have needed rebuilding. A page built around a country took a second study without trouble.

standards.label: Text contrast
standards.value: Calculated from the site’s own colours: navy on white 14.6 to 1, body text 5.6 to 1, and red 4.1 to 1, used for large text only.

standards.label: Editing
standards.value: Countries, studies and findings are entered in forms on a custom WordPress theme.

standards.label: Automated scores
standards.value: None on record. The site’s firewall blocks automated test tools.

projects.next: A stored copy of the data on the site itself, and new study types on the same country page.

proves.title: I use what already works.
proves.text: The research team’s spreadsheet already held the data, so the site reads it directly and nothing was rebuilt.

proves.title: I design for what comes next.
proves.text: One page design took a second study type and now carries 14 country reports.

proves.title: I turn numbers into sentences.
proves.text: Each country page says what the results mean in plain words, written with the research team.

projects.name: Dual Diploma Switzerland
projects.scope: Website design, WordPress build and a multi-step application form
projects.line: Education · 2025 · Built from scratch, in four languages, with a five-step application form.
projects.summary: An American diploma programme had to make sense to Swiss families. I designed and built the site from scratch, in four languages, with an application form that follows the programme’s official structure.

detailImage.alt: The Dual Diploma Switzerland home page: the welcome text on deep green beside a photograph of three students laughing together.
detailImage.caption: The first screen: the two diplomas in yellow on green, with the students beside them.

figures.label: Languages, because Swiss families read German, French, Italian and English
Short steps in the application form, in place of one long page of around 40 details
Credits validated from the Swiss transcript, the sum the site has to explain

origin: The Dual Diploma lets Swiss students earn the American High School Diploma alongside the Swiss Matura or Specialised School Certificate. Academica, the American education group behind it, runs the programme internationally.
The work came to me by referral. Switzerland needed a site of its own, because the offer only makes sense in Swiss terms: cantons, school years and Swiss francs.
There was no site to start from, so I designed and built one from scratch.

intro: Three things about the audience shaped the site.

items.title: Families decide together, over a long time
items.text: This is two to four years of extra study alongside normal school, so the site has to answer detailed questions before anyone applies.

items.title: Switzerland has several school systems
items.text: The programme fits differently by canton, so the site sets out model tables by canton and school year.

items.title: Switzerland has several languages
items.text: In 2023, 66% of residents named German as a main language, 23% French and 8% Italian, while 6% named English. A site in one language would miss most of its families.

intro: A family is trusting a school with years of a child’s study. The design had to look established, and it had to make a complicated offer simple on the first screen.

items.title: Why green and yellow
items.text: The colours come from the Academica crest, so the Swiss site reads as part of an established American institution.

items.title: Why text and photograph sit side by side
items.text: The first screen splits in two: the promise on solid green, the students beside it. Nothing is printed over the photograph, so the words stay sharp on any photo and any screen. White on the green reaches a contrast of 9.9 to 1 and the yellow 7.4 to 1, both past the 7 to 1 of WCAG’s highest level.

items.title: Why the two diplomas get the yellow
items.text: One line on the first screen is in colour: the American High School Diploma and the Swiss Matura. That is the whole offer, so it is what a visitor should remember.

items.title: Why this photograph
items.text: The programme is studied online, and a parent’s natural fear is that online means alone. So the first picture is three students laughing together. In eye-tracking research, Moran Cerf and colleagues found that faces and text draw the eye far more than other parts of an image, so the first screen holds just those two things.

items.title: Why the sum is spelled out
items.text: 24 credits are needed, 18 are validated from the Swiss transcript, and 6 are studied online. The page walks through that sum because it is the main thing a parent has to believe.

items.title: Why Apply Now is always there
items.text: The button sits in the header of every page, so a family that has decided never has to look for it.

intro: The words were written by the client, who knows the families and the Swiss system.

items.title: Why the site uses Swiss terms
items.text: It says Matura, Specialised School Certificate, 10VP/VG and canton of Vaud, because those are the words families use. Prices appear in Swiss francs first, with US dollars beside them.

items.title: How the four languages were made
items.text: The translations were produced with an AI language model, then the German and Italian were corrected by native speakers.

decisions.title: Build a custom theme
decisions.text: A custom WordPress theme lets the client update most of the site without a developer.

decisions.title: Split the form into five steps
decisions.text: The form asks for around 40 details, so it is split into five short steps: student, address, first guardian, second guardian and schooling. Research on the goal-gradient effect (Kivetz and colleagues, 2006) found that people put in more effort as they see themselves getting closer to a goal, and each finished step is visible progress.

decisions.title: Follow the official structure
decisions.text: The form began from the client’s Google Form and was rebuilt in October 2026 to match what Academica International Studies requires.

decisions.title: Send applications to a Swiss address
decisions.text: Every application goes straight to the programme’s own Swiss inbox.

decisions.title: Stay on after launch
decisions.text: I have kept supporting the site since launch, with fee tables, social links, press coverage and canton model tables.

results: A live site in four languages, run day to day by the client, with an application form built to the programme’s official structure.
The programme has been covered in the Swiss newspaper La Côte, and the site links to the article.
lessons: Build for the person who edits the site. The year on the form was fixed inside the form plugin, and the fee table needed a developer to change. Small updates that come round every year should be in the client’s hands from the start.

Build forms from the official rules. The form began from what the client had. When the official structure had to be followed, fields moved and new ones were added. Starting from that structure would have saved the rebuild.
AI translation is a first draft. It gave the site four languages quickly and at low cost, but native speakers still had to correct it. Any translation budget should include that step.

standards.label: Text contrast
standards.value: Calculated from the site’s own colours: white on green 9.9 to 1, and yellow on green 7.4 to 1.

standards.label: Editing
standards.value: Pages are edited in WordPress by the client.

projects.next: Yearly dates and fee tables the client can change without a developer, and new schools and cantons in the model tables.

proves.title: I explain an offer in local terms.
proves.text: An American programme reads as a Swiss one: cantons, school years and Swiss francs, in four languages.

proves.title: I make long forms feel short.
proves.text: Around 40 details became five short steps that follow the programme’s official structure.

proves.title: I stay after launch.
proves.text: The site has kept changing with the programme, with fee tables, form changes and press coverage added since it went live.

insights.title: How to write a website brief agencies can quote accurately
insights.summary: What to count, what to name and what to decide before a website brief goes out, so the proposals that come back can be compared.
inShort: When quotes come back far apart, each agency has usually guessed at something the brief left out.
Count the page types, the content that has to move, the languages and the connections to other systems.
State your budget range and your scoring in the brief itself.
insights.lead: When three proposals for the same website come back far apart, it rarely means that two agencies are wrong. It usually means each one guessed at something the brief left out. This piece is for the programme or communications officer who has to write the terms of reference and then compare what comes back.

body.text: What a terms of reference is for

The United Nations Procurement Manual describes a terms of reference as “a description of the scope of work for services, generally indicating the work to be performed, the level of quality and effort, the timeline, and the deliverables”. It adds that the document is often a vendor’s first and main introduction to what you need, and that clear terms limit the risk on both sides.

The Manual warns in both directions. Over-specification “may increase prices and/or decrease the number of offers”. Under-specification is the opposite failure: essential information is left out. For a website, that second failure is the expensive one. An agency that cannot see how much content has to move will either add a large margin for it or quote low and come back later.
When two quotes differ, ask what each agency assumed. The gap is usually in the brief.
What to count before you send it

items: Page types, not pages. List the templates you need: home, article, document, event, country. Design and build cost follows the number of types, not the number of pages.
What has to move. How many pages and documents are on the current site, and which can stay behind. Count them from the content system if you can, because a crawl misses what is not linked.
Languages. Which ones at launch, which later, whether any read right to left, and who does the translating.
Connections. Name each outside system: payments, mailing list, dashboards, single sign-on. Say who holds each account.
Editors. How many people will update the site, how often, and how much training they need.
Standards. The accessibility level, a page-weight limit, where the site may be hosted, and any data protection rules.

body.text: Say how you will decide

The Manual says solicitation documents must state the evaluation criteria, and that the balance between technical and commercial scoring must be set before a request for proposals goes out. Follow that even if your own rules do not require it. Agencies write better proposals when they know what will be scored.

Then give a budget range. It does not weaken your position. It tells each agency what level of work to propose, so you compare answers to the same question. Hold one round of questions, and share every answer with every bidder.

sources.title: United Nations Procurement Manual (DOS/2020.9), United Nations Department of Operational Support, 2020

insights.title: A performance budget for sites read on slow connections
insights.summary: How to set a page-weight limit before design starts, and how to measure it so the number means something on a phone with a weak signal.
inShort: Set a page-weight limit before design starts, and treat it as a requirement.
I work to 500 KB a page: about ten seconds at 400 kilobits per second.
Measure each page as it opens, scrolled to the end, and on a high-density phone.
insights.lead: Field staff often open a website on a phone, on a weak signal, in the middle of something else. If the page takes a minute, it does not get read. This piece is for teams commissioning or building a site for people in low-bandwidth settings, and it sets out how I choose a limit and hold to it.

body.text: Pick the number first

web.dev defines a performance budget as “a set of limits imposed on metrics that affect site performance”. Its suggested starting point is under 170 KB of critical-path resources and under five seconds to interactive, worked out for baseline devices on a 3G network.

Compare that with the web as it is. The HTTP Archive’s Web Almanac put the median home page in 2025 at 2.86 MB on desktop and 2.56 MB on mobile. On a slow connection of 400 kilobits per second, 2.56 MB takes about 51 seconds to arrive, before any delay from the network itself.

I work to 500 KB a page. That is about ten seconds at the same speed: slow, but usable. It leaves room for one good photograph and a set of web fonts, which matters when the site also has to look like the organisation that runs it.
A budget nobody checks is a wish. It has to be measured, on every release, by someone who can stop the release.
Measure it the way it will fail
A single figure from a desktop browser hides most of the problem. These are the checks that have caught real overruns on my projects:

items: As it opens. Use an empty cache and count the bytes that travel, not the size of the files on the server.
Scrolled to the end. Lazy loading delays images, it does not remove them. A page can pass as it opens and fail by the bottom.
On a high-density phone. Two-times and three-times screens ask for larger images, so the same page can weigh far more than it does on a laptop.
With JavaScript off. Lazy loading that depends on a script stops, and every image on the page may load at once.

body.text: Put it in the contract

Write the limit into the brief, with the method for measuring it. Then each new feature has a price the whole team can see. When something goes over, web.dev gives the three honest choices: optimise it, remove it, or do not add it.
The discipline pays for itself in the first emergency that sends a new audience to the site on phones and poor connections. By then it is too late to start.

insights.title: Accessible colour that keeps a brand recognisable
insights.summary: Why most brand palettes fail only in particular pairings, and how giving each colour a job keeps both the brand and the contrast ratio.
inShort: Brand colours rarely fail everywhere. They fail at small sizes and in particular pairings.
Body text needs 4.5:1. Large text and interface parts need 3:1.
Give each colour a job, and test every pair it will appear in.
insights.lead: Accessibility and branding are often set against each other, as if one has to give way. The real problem is much narrower. This piece is for communications teams and designers who own a palette and have been told it fails.

body.text: What the standard asks for

WCAG 2.2 asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for text, and 3:1 for large text, which it defines as at least 18 point, or 14 point bold. User interface components and meaningful graphics need 3:1 against what sits next to them. Colour also cannot be the only way information is shown. Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement.
This is the most common failure there is. WebAIM’s 2026 study of the top million home pages found low-contrast text on 83.9% of them, with an average of 34 instances a page.
Most palettes do not fail. Particular pairings fail.
What that looks like on a real palette

My own logo uses six colours, one for each language the site speaks. Against white, the blue measures 6.16:1, the violet 5.72:1 and the pink 4.84:1, so all three could carry body text. The orange measures 4.30:1, the green 4.38:1 and the amber 3.65:1. Those three fail for small text and pass for large text.

I did not change the colours. I changed their jobs. All six appear in the logo, and the display at the top of the home page is set in one of them. All the small text on the site is near-black or dark grey, at 7.23:1 or better. The brand keeps its colour, and no one has to read 14-pixel amber.
How to check a palette

items: List every pair: each text colour on each background it will sit on, including hover states and text over photographs.
Mark each pair as good for body text, good for large text only, or failing.
Give each colour a job from that table: text, display, fill or decoration.
Where a colour has to carry small text, darken it slightly rather than replacing it. Readers recognise the hue, not the exact value.
Find what colour alone is saying, such as links, errors and chart lines, and add an underline, an icon or a label.

body.text: Write it down

A palette survives handover when the guidelines say what each colour may do, not only what its value is. Put the table in the brand guide. The next person to build a campaign page will not have to work it out, and the brand will still look like itself.

intro: Most organisations I work with publish in several languages to readers who have nothing in common except the site: a coordinator on a phone in the field, a donor’s adviser in Geneva, a journalist, a ministry. Design that serves all of them cannot start from a look. It starts from a map of who the site is for and what each of them needs to do.

Then I prototype the real thing early. You review working pages on real screens, pin comments to them, and approve a prototype you have clicked through before anything is built. Decisions are made on an interface, not on pictures of one.

What you receive is a design system: colour tokens, type, components and their states, documented so that engineering implements it without interpretation and so that it holds across six scripts, including right-to-left. The Collective Service runs 30 page templates from one such system.

Evidence intelligence is a knowledge layer built on everything your organisation holds. A reader describes a situation in their own words and receives an answer drawn only from your material, with every statement traced to the passage it came from. When your material has no answer, it says so.
